newsitem.title: USA: Shuttle crew gear up for satellite release.
newsitem.headline: Shuttle crew gear up for satellite release.

text.p: The crew of the space shuttle Columbia prepared on Friday to release a satellite designed to manufacture ultra-pure components for the electronics industry.

Astronaut Tom Jones, using the shuttle's robot arm, was to set free the Wake Shield Facility at about 8:11 p.m. EST Friday (0111 GMT Saturday). Jones lifted the satellite out of the shuttle's cargo bay on Friday afternoon in readiness for its deployment.

The Wake Shield is designed to manufacture ultra-pure semiconductors for use in high-speed computer chips. The stainless steel, saucer-shaped spacecraft could eventually lead to the first commercial space factories, its designers said.

As the Wake Shield travels through the atmosphere 218 miles (350 km) up, the 12-foot (3.5-meter) diameter disc will create a vacuum behind the craft nearly 100 times better than that possible on earth.
The near-perfect vacuum will provide ideal conditions for the atom-by-atom manufacture of semiconductors, free of the contamination found in ground-based laboratories.

"It may make materials that are needed for high performance computers, for wireless radio communications or cellular phones," Jones said. "All of these kinds of high performance chips that we need for our electronic information-age society might be able to be made more cheaply in space. The Wake Shield is a way to test that hypothesis."
The Wake Shield will fly about 35 miles (56 km) behind Columbia for three days before the shuttle crew returns on Monday night to pick it up.

The University of Houston Space Vacuum Epitaxy Center and Space Industries Inc., which designed the Wake Shield, have made about $5 million in improvements to solve the technical problems which plagued its first two test flights.
On the Wake Shield's maiden flight in January 1994, problems with the attitude control system prevented its deployment; it remained on the end of the shuttle's robot arm.
The spacecraft was released into orbit on its second mission in September 1995, but it suffered further attitude problems and its electronics overheated.
Despite the problems, the Wake Shield manufactured four of the seven planned semiconductor wafers. Project officials said the quality was far superior to ground-manufactured wafers.
It will be make or break for the Wake Shield as this is its final planned outing. NASA recently cancelled a fourth test flight to make way for another shuttle visit to the Mir space station.
"We believe this is going to be a very successful flight this time around," Alex Ignatiev, director of the Space Vacuum Epitaxy Center, said.

The Wake Shield will be the second recoverable satellite deployed on this mission. A U.S.-German telescope was released from Columbia on Tuesday night and was continuing on Friday to make observations of the mysterious interstellar matter that lies between the stars.
